title: Cerebellar Neurons
intro: The cerebellum holds more than half of the brain's neurons in a crystalline circuit that repeats almost unchanged across its whole surface. Its few cell types (granule, Purkinje, Golgi, stellate, basket, deep nuclear and inferior olive neurons) are some of the best characterised in neuroscience, and the circuit has had a precise computational theory since Marr (1969) and Albus (1971): a supervised learning machine that uses error signals to adjust a huge expansion of its input.

blocks.text: Mossy fibres carry sensory, motor and cortical context into the granule layer, where a vast population of tiny granule cells recodes it. Their axons, the parallel fibres, run along the folia and cross the flat dendritic trees of hundreds of Purkinje cells. Each Purkinje cell also receives one climbing fibre from the inferior olive, which fires about once a second and is thought to signal errors. When a climbing fibre spike coincides with parallel fibre input, those parallel fibre synapses are depressed (cerebellar LTD; Ito & Kano 1982). Purkinje cells, the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei, which send the cerebellum's output to the rest of the brain.

items: Expansion recoding: the granule layer maps a few thousand mossy fibre signals onto billions of granule cells, each sampling only about four mossy fibres, making input patterns more separable (like the dentate gyrus and the insect mushroom body).
Perceptron-like learning: each Purkinje cell is a perceptron over its parallel fibre inputs, trained by a teaching signal (the climbing fibre).
Error-driven plasticity: climbing fibre activity signals that a movement was wrong; the depression of co-active parallel fibre synapses changes the Purkinje output next time.

Evidence: classic eyeblink conditioning and adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex depend on this circuit (Ito 1984; Medina et al. 2000). Many forms of plasticity beyond parallel fibre LTD are now known, including potentiation and plasticity in the nuclei (Gao, van Beugen & De Zeeuw 2012).
Purkinje Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cerebellar/purkinje): huge flat dendritic trees, simple and complex spikes, the De Schutter-Bower model.
Cerebellar Granule Cells (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cerebellar/cerebellar-granule): the most numerous neurons in the brain, a four-input expansion layer.
Inferior Olive Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cerebellar/inferior-olive): electrically coupled oscillators that produce the climbing fibre teaching signal.

Deep Cerebellar Nuclei Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/cerebellar/deep-cerebellar-nuclei): the cerebellum's output cells, pacemakers shaped by Purkinje inhibition, with rebound firing and a second site of learning.
Adaptive filter models (Fujita 1982; Dean et al. 2010): the granule layer as a bank of temporal filters, the Purkinje cell as a weighted sum trained by a decorrelation (LMS-like) rule.

Spiking network models: Medina and Mauk (2000) simulated eyeblink conditioning with a spiking cerebellar network; Yamazaki and Tanaka (2007) built a granule layer that encodes the passage of time; the Blue Brain-like reconstructions of the granular layer by D'Angelo and colleagues (Solinas et al. 2010; Casali et al. 2019) and the cerebellar scaffold model use detailed models of each cell type.
Neuromorphic and robotic implementations: cerebellar controllers on SpiNNaker and in robot arms (Carrillo et al. 2008; Luque et al. 2011) use simplified spiking versions of the same cell types.
